extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of American constitutional government (undergraduate/graduate level)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and assessing normative criteria and institutional features that determine the functioning, independence, and legitimacy of courts (especially the U.S. Supreme Court) and comparing them to parliamentary/cabinet systems. Useful for evaluating judicial design, administration, and behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supreme Court as the 'living voice' of the Constitution
rubrics_metrics.description: The Supreme court is the living voice of the Constitution — the conscience of the people and the guarantee of the minority; it interprets and enforces the fundamental law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To discharge these momentous functions the court must be stable even as the Constitution is stable. Its spirit and tone must be that of the people at their best moments. It must resist transitory impulses and the seductions of popular sentiment, and be able to defy attacks from other government departments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stability versus correction of past decisions (precedent management)
rubrics_metrics.description: The court must choose between unsettling the law by reversing former decisions and perpetuating bad law by following them; it has not always followed its own former decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When constitutional words are plain or prior cases are decisive the court must follow them. Where terms admit more than one construction or previous decisions leave the true construction open, a court may prefer the construction suited to the needs of the time and may, in extreme cases, reverse prior decisions. Public opinion may influence such shifts (example: the Granger cases).

rubrics_metrics.name: Independence of the judiciary (life tenure and salary protection)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Framers secured the complete independence of the judiciary by preventing the President from removing judges and Congress from diminishing their salaries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This structural independence is central, but it is imperfect because the Constitution does not fix the number of justices; Congress can change the court's size, creating a vulnerability (court-packing) as shown by historical examples (e.g., 1801, 1866, 1869).

rubrics_metrics.name: Vulnerability from changing court size and political manipulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Because the Constitution does not fix the number of Supreme Court justices, Congress may increase or diminish their number and thus potentially alter the court's character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical instances (Congress abolished circuit courts in 1801, reduced Supreme Court seats in 1866 to block appointments, then raised number in 1869) illustrate how altering court size can be used politically to outvote incumbent justices and undermine constitutional protections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial appointments and (non-)partisanship
rubrics_metrics.description: Federal judgeships have hitherto been given to members of the President's party and usually to persons resident in the State(s) where the court sits; non-political appointments are occasionally made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although cases of corruption are practically unknown and partisanship is infrequent, appointments often reflect political affiliation and local residency; this influences the court's composition and tendencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative adequacy: salaries, staffing, and docket management
rubrics_metrics.description: Chief defects in the courts have been inadequate salaries and insufficient staff in populous commercial States, producing backlogs and long delays (e.g., sometimes three years from entry to hearing in the Supreme Court).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposed remedies include limiting the right of appeal to cases involving considerable sums of money or dividing the Supreme Court into divisional courts for ordinary suits while reserving constitutional questions for the full court.

rubrics_metrics.name: Influence of public opinion on judicial decision-making
rubrics_metrics.description: The Supreme Court feels the touch of public opinion; judges are only men and may yield prudently to popular sentiment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public opinion can be a grounding for presuming correctness because it expresses the progressive judgment of the world, but it must not displace clear constitutional text or controlling precedent. At times pervasive public sympathy has been irresistible (illustrated by the Granger decisions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial temperament shaped by pre-bench beliefs
rubrics_metrics.description: The court's temper and tendencies change over time according to the political proclivities and pre-existing habits of thought of the men who compose it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Change is usually slow because vacancies are rare; the court's actions often flow from the judges' prior convictions rather than conscious partisan prostitution of functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparative rule: judicial review versus parliamentary sovereignty
rubrics_metrics.description: In many European (cabinet/parliamentary) systems the legislature is sovereign and courts do not entertain questions of the validity of legislative acts; the judiciary does not enter into the political part of government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: By contrast, the U.S. system creates a Supreme Court empowered to interpret the Constitution and resolve inter-branch disputes; this is a structural difference with implications for the balance of powers and the protection of minorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design rules to prevent executive encroachment (separation safeguards)
rubrics_metrics.description: To prevent executive influence, the Framers forbade persons holding office under the United States from being members of either House and chose an indirect popular election mechanism (electors) for the President to make him independent of Congress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These rules were intended to render the legislature pure and independent and to balance powers between Congress and President. The trade-off is potential weakness in each branch (e.g., a President fettered in foreign policy/appointments and a divided Congress weakened by bicameralism).

rubrics_metrics.name: Trade-off between independence and effective government
rubrics_metrics.description: The separation of powers makes each branch independent but can also make them weak in their own spheres (e.g., President fettered by Senate rights and forbidden to appeal to the country; Congress weakened by two equal houses).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While independence protects liberty, it may produce paralysis or inefficiency; the design balances preventing arbitrary power against the danger of a feeble executive or legislative deadlock.

rubrics_metrics.name: People's vigilance as the ultimate safeguard of constitutional order
rubrics_metrics.description: When constitutional forms are legally manipulated or distorted, the principal protection is the fear and judgment of the people; their wisdom and self-restraint are ultimately relied on to condemn perversions of constitutional form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If public excitement rises and a majority acquiesces, formal legality may be used to achieve revolutionary ends; therefore popular opinion and civic virtue are essential backstops to institutional checks.
